bib.title: A Pretrainer's Guide to Training Data: Measuring the Effects of Data Age, Domain Coverage, Quality, & Toxicity

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only; first lines of Appendix A (related work) sit in the references block and were read in the context of the lineage.

question: How do pretraining data age, source-domain composition, and quality and toxicity filtering each change downstream performance and toxic behaviour of language models?
contributions: Pretrain 28 distinct 1.5B decoder-only models from scratch on C4 and Pile variants, the largest publicly documented pretraining-data ablation study per the authors
Show pretraining-evaluation temporal misalignment degrades performance and is not removed by finetuning
Quantify quality and toxicity filter effects, showing a trade-off between benchmark performance and toxic generation
Ablate Pile source domains one at a time and show heterogeneous web and books data matter most
Recommend reporting the temporal distribution of pretraining data and treating curation policy as a hyperparameter

method.summary: Decoder-only LMs (LM-XL 1.5B, LM-SMALL 20M) are pretrained from scratch with T5X on variants of C4 (four Common Crawl years, quality-filtered, toxicity-filtered) and the Pile (one of nine domains removed at a time). Each is finetuned per task and evaluated on temporal, QA, toxicity identification and toxic generation benchmarks, with scores reported relative to the unfiltered model.
method.task: next-token pretraining data ablation, evaluated by finetuning on QA, toxicity identification, temporal classification/summarisation, plus toxic generation without finetuning

models.name: LM-XL
models.architecture: decoder-only Transformer similar to t5.1.1-XL config, causal decoding with full LM objective, prefix LM objective for finetuning

training.objective: autoregressive next-token prediction (full language modeling) for pretraining; prefix LM for finetuning
training.lr_schedule: decay factor 0.5, 20000 steps per decay (Table 7); defaults from Wang et al. 2022
training.tokens: inferred: 4096 x 512 x 88,064 = about 185B tokens seen, from Table 7
training.hardware: TPUs, 8x8x8 for LM-XL, 8x8 for LM-SMALL (T5X, TensorFlow)
training.seeds: single run per configuration; authors call these single-shot experiments

other.finetune_toxicity_identification: seq 128, batch 128, dropout 0.1, lr 1e-3, 10k steps (LM-XL), 30k (LM-SMALL), TPU 8x8, AUC-ROC
other.finetune_natural_questions: seq 512, batch 128, dropout 0.1, lr 1e-3, 50k steps, accuracy
other.finetune_time_tasks: 4x4 TPUs, batch 64, max seq 128, validate every 500 steps, test score at best validation accuracy; lr and steps per Table 10 (e.g. PubCLS LM-XL 1e-4 30k; NewSum 5e-4 40k; PoliAff 1e-4 15k; TwiERC 1e-4 30k; AIC 1e-4 30k)
other.note: Table 8 and the text say 'Natural Qs' and 'Acc (By Dataset)'; finetuning optimizer not stated

inference.samples: 25 responses per prompt for RealToxicityPrompts; 50 responses per prompt for Representational Bias
inference.prompting: no prompting study; standard prompts of each downstream dataset used for finetuning

parameters.toxic_threshold: Perspective score >= 0.5 marks a response toxic

metrics.name: Temporal Degradation (TD)
metrics.definition: performance change from one year of misalignment (Luu et al. 2022), extended to pretraining-year versus evaluation-year, comparing only runs with the same finetuning and evaluation years; averaged over evaluation years

metrics.name: Pearson r
metrics.definition: correlation between temporal misalignment and performance change; one-sided Wald test on slope

metrics.name: QA F1 by domain
metrics.definition: average F1 per domain category of MRQA/UnifiedQA datasets, reported as relative change vs unfiltered model

metrics.name: Toxicity identification AUC-ROC
metrics.definition: AUC-ROC on SBF, Toxigen, DynaHate R3 and R4 test sets; Score is mean change vs full dataset

metrics.name: Toxic generation RTP-T / RTP-NT / RepBias
metrics.definition: probability that one of the generations per prompt has Perspective toxicity >= 0.5, for toxic and non-toxic prompts; RepBias averaged per identity marker with 95% CI

baselines: model pretrained on the unfiltered/full dataset
oldest or other pretraining years (age study)
one-at-a-time domain removal vs full Pile
eval.protocol: Each pretrained model is finetuned separately per task and evaluated on default splits, so differences are attributed to pretraining; scores are relative to the unfiltered baseline. No seeds or repeated runs.

availability.data: C4 and the Pile are public; the quality classifier is proprietary (PaLM/GLaM)

results.claim: Quality filtering improves most QA categories by 1-6% despite removing 10%+ of the training data.
results.setup: LM-XL, C4, quality classifier thresholds, relative QA performance

results.claim: Quality filter at T=0.975 keeps 91% of C4 and raises average relative QA performance by 2.5.
Inverse quality filter (removing the highest-quality 27%) lowers average QA performance by 3.1.
results.table: Table 3, row Inv T=0.5, column Avg

results.claim: Toxicity filter at T=0.5 lowers average QA performance by 2.7 while keeping 76% of data.
Strongest toxicity filter (T=0.3) cuts RTP-T toxic generation from 84.6 to 55.0 on C4 but lowers toxicity identification by 5.2.
results.table: Table 15, C4 row T=0.3, columns RTP-T and Score

results.claim: Inverse toxicity filter T=0.06 gives the best toxicity identification, +1.4 over full data on Pile.
results.table: Table 15, Pile row INVERSE T=0.06, column Score

results.claim: Quality filtering at T=0.9 raises RepBias toxic generation score by 11.1 percent relative to unfiltered C4.
Removing Common Crawl (26.9% of the Pile) causes the largest decreases in both toxicity generation and identification among domain ablations.
results.table: Table 17, row NO CC, column Score -1.9

results.claim: The paper states removing Books, CC or OpenWeb gives the largest decreases in toxicity generation and identification.
The Pile's Books domain has 4.3x mean profanity and 1.9x text quality, explaining why high-toxicity documents score high on quality.
results.table: Figure 7, column Books, rows Profanity 4.3x and Text Quality 1.9x

results.claim: Older BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2 and T5 variants account for about 58% of Hugging Face model downloads (April 2023).
The study spans 28 unique 1.5B models pretrained from scratch.
results.note: Abstract text is 'Spanning 28 unique 1.5 billion parameter models'

results.claim: Larger models show more temporal degradation from pretraining than small ones; effect is asymmetric, steeper when evaluation year is after pretraining year.

results.claim: Best QA performance still comes from models pretrained on all or nearly all sources; heterogeneous sources beat targeted data.

limits: English only, two datasets (C4, Pile); authors say composition matters more for multilingual models
Single-shot runs: no seeds or repeats because of compute cost; compute and wall-clock not reported
Quality and toxicity are defined only by classifier output (PaLM quality classifier, Perspective API); Perspective is a black box shown by Pozzobon et al. 2023 to shift over time
Quality classifier is proprietary, so filter is not reproducible
Models and code not released for organisational reasons
Only finetuned settings studied, not zero/few-shot prompting; 1.5B scale only (20M for scaling of temporal effect)
Newer datasets (RefinedWeb, Dolma, RedPajama) postdate the experiments; authors expect findings to generalise
Domain ablations conflate removed domain with reduced data size, as the authors note for toxicity filters (decrease may be due to less training data)
Mismatch noted: Section 2.3 says 27 QA datasets, Appendix D says 30

terms.definition: the performance change observed from a one year difference between the finetuning and evaluation years (Luu et al. 2022), generalised here to pretraining versus evaluation year
a filter that removes the least toxic (or highest quality) documents below a threshold instead of the most
